'''Anatole Beck''' (19 March 1930 – 21 December 2014)<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: Anatole Beck|url=http://www.math.wisc.edu/anatole-beck|website=University of Wisconsin Department of Mathematics|date=27 October 2022 }}</ref> was an American mathematician.

== Education and academic career ==
Beck graduated from [[Stuyvesant High School]] in 1947,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mojo-working.com/Math1946F.html|title=Stuyvesant High School Math Team 1946}}</ref> studied at [[Brooklyn College]] (Bachelor's degree 1951) and in 1956 received his PhD from [[Yale University]] under [[Shizuo Kakutani]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Mathematics Genealogy Project - Anatole Beck|url=http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=8420|website=Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref> In 1958 he became Assistant Professor and in 1966 Professor in the [http://math.wisc.edu Department of Mathematics] at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]. He married Jewish feminist writer [[Evelyn Torton Beck]] in 1954; they had two children before divorcing in 1974.<ref>"Evelyn Torton Beck," ''Jewish Women's Archive'',  https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/beck-evelyn-torton</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Teacher Commutes via Jet |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/38126352/evelyn_torton_beck_born_1933/ |newspaper=Wisconsin State Journal |date=March 26, 1972 |page=62 |via = [[Newspapers.com]] |accessdate=October 30, 2019}} {{Open access}}</ref> He met his second wife Eve-Lynn Siegel Beck in 1998, she was cousins with Michael Bleicher, one of Anatole’s longtime friends.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Zepeda|first=L|date=27 April 2021|title=Anatole Beck: Meritorious Service|url=http://www.wuu.info/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/AnatoleApril28.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=28 April 2021|website=Wisconsin University Union|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428181800/http://www.wuu.info/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/AnatoleApril28.pdf |archive-date=2021-04-28 }}</ref>

He was a visiting professor at the [[Technical University of Munich]], the [[London School of Economics]] and a visiting scholar at the [[University of Göttingen]], [[University of Warwick]], [[University of London]], and the [[Hebrew University]].

Beck's work dealt with [[ergodic theory]], [[topological dynamics]], [[Probability]] in [[Banach spaces]], [[measure theory]], [[search theory]], [[linear search problem]], and mathematics in the social sciences.

== Union leadership, political activism, and social commentator ==
Beck was an ardent supporter of [[trade union|unionism]] and [[cooperative economics]], helping to found the faculty union chapter at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and serving as the Vice President of the [[American Federation of Teachers|Wisconsin Federation of Teachers]]. He spoke out strongly in favor of academic freedom on campus, and was an early supporter of the free speech rights of the movement against the [[Vietnam War]] in the 1960s. He witnessed the “[[List of protests against the Vietnam War|Dow Riots]]” of October 18, 1967 in the Commerce Building (now Ingraham Hall), condemning the police violence against students at a faculty meeting.<ref name=":1" /> Beck made headlines in 1977 when he offered a $100 grant to a "white Quaker female student with financial need" to highlight the University of Wisconsin's policy of accepting gifts with discriminatory conditions attached.<ref>{{cite news|title=UW Prof Won't Lift Gift Conditions |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/38070539/anatole_beck_19302014/ |newspaper=Wisconsin State Journal |date=August 27, 1977 |page=1 |via = [[Newspapers.com]] |accessdate=October 29, 2019}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Stick to Your Guns, Professor |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/38070607/anatole_beck_19302014/ |newspaper=The Capital Times |date=September 3, 1977 |page=1 |via = [[Newspapers.com]] |accessdate=October 29, 2019}} {{Open access}}</ref>  Around 1980 he and Jim Donnelly founded [http://www.wuu.info/ Wisconsin University Union] (WUU) which focused on promoting shared governance and academic freedom.<ref name=":0" />

Beck was interested in solving social problems. In 1996 he wrote “[https://www.math.wisc.edu/beck/2k.htm The Knowledge Business]” advocating for investment in education, universal public preschools with adequate stimulation and nutrition.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Beck|first=Anatole|date=1996|title=The Knowledge Business|url=https://www.math.wisc.edu/beck/2k.htm|url-status=live|access-date=28 April 2021|website=University of Wisconsin Mathematics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428181808/https://www.math.wisc.edu/beck/2k.htm |archive-date=2021-04-28 }}</ref>  Ahead of his time, he argued for free public transportation, advocated for greater leisure, and a universal basic income from what he called the “knowledge dividend” from all past knowledge and innovation.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> Arguing against overtime for some and unemployment for other, he predicted that, unchecked, companies would offer little stability, longer hours and create a global economy of “exoslavery,” where the conditions of slavery could be moved to other countries.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />  He condemned economists for calling this rational and free trade, predicting increases in underemployment, homelessness, a rise in TB, and disinvestment in basic research, among other things. He also called for a tax on security transactions, now called a [[Tobin tax]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> Beginning in 2008 he was a commentator on the Insurgent Radio Kiosk on Madison's community radio station WORT.<ref>{{cite web|title=anatole beck commentaries|url=http://abeckcomment.blogspot.com/}}</ref>

In 2009 Beck was interviewed extensively by Robert Lange for the UW-Madison Oral History Program.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=Oral History Interview: Anatole Beck (1057)|date=September 2009 |url=http://minds.wisconsin.edu/handle/1793/65670 |last1=Lange |first1=Robert |last2=Beck |first2=Anatole }}</ref>

== Headlines ==
* Michael N. Bleicher, Donald W. Crowe: Excursions into Mathematics, AK Peters, 2000 (first 1967)
* Continuous flow in the plane, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften, Springer Verlag, 1974 (participation Mirit and Jonathan Lewin)
* with M. Bleicher: Packing convex sets into a similar set in Konrad Jacobs: Selecta Mathematica, Volume 3, Springer Verlag 1971
* A paradox. The Tortoise and the Hare, in Konrad Jacobs: Selecta Mathematica, Volume 5, Springer Verlag 1979
